transcript:
## City of Somerville, Massachusetts City Council Public Health and Public Safety Committee Meeting Minutes

Tuesday, November 10, 2026

6:30 PM

This meeting was held via Zoom and was called to order by Chair McLaughlin at 6:33 pm and adjourned at 7:59 pm on a roll call vote of 3 in favor (Councilors Mbah, Clingan and McLaughlin), 0 opposed, and 0 absent.

Also present: Amanda Nagim-Williams — Director of Intergovernmental Affairs (IGA), Karin Carroll — Director of Health and Human Services, Colin Zeigler — Public Health Division Director, Ben Wheeler — City Councilor at Large and Delaney Fisher-Cassiol — Clerk of Committees

Roll Call

- Present: City Councilor At Large Wilfred N. Mbah, Ward Four City
- Councilor Jesse Clingan and Ward One City Councilor
- Matthew McLaughlin

1. Committee

Approval of the Minutes of the Public Health and Public Safety Committee

Minutes

Meeting of September 30, 2026.

(ID # 26-1516 )

- RESULT: ACCEPTED
- AYE:

- City Councilor At Large Mbah, Ward Four City Councilor
- Clingan and Ward One City Councilor McLaughlin

2. Resolution

By Councilor Link and Councilor McLaughlin

(ID # 26-1500 ) In support of meeting spaces for Alcoholics Anonymous.

- Intergovernmental Affairs Director Amanda Nagim-Williams reported that
- four Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) groups previously met at the Ralph and

Jenny Center on Washington Street. Following the City's acquisition of the building, staff worked to relocate the groups to St. James Episcopal Church. Three have secured a meeting space there, while the fourth is still looking because St. James Episcopal Church was unavailable at the time needed.

- Staff also worked with the church to relax parking requirements to better

accommodate the groups. Director Nagim-Williams noted that the Property and Tenant Manager worked closely with the groups to identify and tour

potential spaces to ensure they met their needs. She added that maintaining access to the Ralph and Jenny Center outside regular hours would have

- required additional staff to open and close the building and provide security.

- The relocations were coordinated to avoid any interruption in the groups'
- meetings.

Councilor Clingan expressed concern that the groups had been displaced and noted that there are increasingly fewer spaces available for these types of meetings. Councilor Mbah emphasized the importance of accessible, consistent meeting spaces, noting that recovery requires community support

and resources. He asked whether libraries or schools could be considered as alternatives. Director Nagim-Williams explained that these locations could

present similar challenges related to staffing, building access and cleaning, as well as potential conflicts with City programming. Councilor Clingan

suggested exploring the Cummings schools, which may already have staff on site during evening hours. Director Nagim-Williams agreed to follow up

- on this possibility.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE MARKED WORK

COMPLETED

3. Public

Barbara Phillips submitting comments re: Warming Center.

Communication

(ID # 26-1478 )

This item was discussed with item #26-1305.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE MARKED WORK

COMPLETED

4. Order

By Councilor Wheeler, Councilor Hardt and Councilor Sait

(ID # 26-1421 ) That, in view of the proliferation of rats in the city, the Director of Public

- Health and/or designees update this Council on the status of dumpster

license registration and enforcement, including: estimates of the numbers of licensed and unlicensed dumpsters in the city which regularly contain

discarded food; procedures for identifying unlicensed dumpsters and encouraging licensing; criteria for approval of dumpsters; staff capacity for dumpster inspection and enforcement; and current methods and best

- practices for excluding rodents from dumpsters.

Colin Zeigler, Public Health Division Director, reported that 603 dumpsters are actively licensed or in the licensing process, while 14 known dumpsters remain unlicensed. Enforcement is primarily complaint-driven, with the Division auditing businesses that have not renewed their licenses or have

been reported as potentially unlicensed. Notices are issued annually, followed by additional notices before ticketing begins in mid-July. The

- number of unlicensed dumpsters has decreased from 69 in early August to

14. The Division will continue outreach and enforcement. Compliance requirements include properly fitted lids, preventing rodent access, accessible drain plugs, undamaged dumpsters and proper overflow practices.

Director Zeigler emphasized that the goal is compliance and education, with best practices including regular cleaning with a 1:9 bleach-to-water solution, more frequent pickups, replacing damaged dumpsters and maintaining

regular pest control. The Division is also working to establish consistent enforcement guidelines.

- Councilor Clingan asked how businesses are informed of dumpster

requirements. Director Zeigler explained that new applicants receive informational materials and that businesses applying for food licenses are

also advised of the dumpster licensing requirement. Councilor Clingan also suggested requiring photos of dumpsters during license renewals. Director

Zeigler noted that, beginning July 1, Code Enforcement Officers are primarily focused on dumpster compliance and that the Division can explore

additional technology to streamline audits, such as requiring photos. In response to Councilor Mbah, he explained that audits are largely reactive

rather than proactive due to staffing constraints and inspectors' existing workloads.

- Councilor Ben Wheeler expressed support for the City's efforts and asked
- about opportunities to coordinate regionally on rodent issues. Director
- Zeigler noted that the City participates in a monthly working group with

Cambridge to share best practices and is exploring new tools to assist inspectors. Councilor Wheeler also raised concerns about dumpster designs

with ridges or gaps that allow rodent access and suggested sharing common design issues with haulers. Councilor Zeigler welcomed the suggestion, noting that the Division typically works with businesses rather than directly with haulers. Councilor Wheeler asked why compliance issues persist.

Zeigler explained that fines are capped at $300 per violation, which may not deter repeat offenders. He also noted that investigating and issuing

violations is time-intensive for inspectors, prompting the Division to consider more efficient enforcement approaches. Councilor Wheeler also

suggested making the City's existing internal map of long-term noncompliant dumpsters publicly available.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE MARKED WORK

COMPLETED

5. Officer's

Director of Emergency Management conveying the 2025-2026 Cummings

Communication School Winter Warming Center After Action Report and Improvement Plan.

(ID # 26-1339 )

This item was discussed with item #26-1305.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE MARKED WORK

COMPLETED

6. Resolution

By Councilor Strezo

(ID # 26-1305 ) That the Director of Health and Human Services discuss the street

- harassment reported by abutters and pedestrians on Prescott Street, School

Street and the area surrounding the Warming Center (when it is open) and what steps are being taken to address this going forward.

Bill Fisher, Director of Emergency Management, reviewed the attachment

PHPS - 2026-11-10 WC AARIP Presentation (with 26-1339). He reported

that the warming center has a new security company and increased capacity.

This past year, nearby residents reported slightly lower satisfaction with the warming center, while clients expressed high satisfaction, particularly with staff helpfulness. The City conducted a 10-year temperature study to determine the warming center's operating dates for this year. This year, the staging area will move to the School Street parking lot, slightly separated from the community and roadway, which is expected to reduce harassment

- and noise. Regarding suggestions to discourage people from lining up early,

Director Fisher explained that clients are often anxious to ensure they have a place to stay that evening. The City is also working to install benches in the parking lot in response to a community request and has increased

transportation services, including shuttle access to a transportation hub to help clients get around during the day. Language access will also be

maintained. Additional information is available at somervillema.gov/warmingcenter or by emailing

warmingcenter@somervillema.gov. Director Fisher encouraged community members to reach out with concerns about the center and to call 911 if they observe an immediate safety risk. He emphasized the importance of addressing behavioral concerns involving specific individuals rather than

- making assumptions about the broader population.

- Councilor Mbah expressed support for the cross-departmental coordination

and encouraged a consistent, intentional, evidence-based response to concerning behavior. Councilor Clingan noted the significant support and attention being given to the warming center and expressed appreciation. In

response to questions from a community member and Councilor Clingan about vendor arrangements, Karin Carroll, Director of Health and Human

Services, explained that the City must wait for funds to be appropriated before securing vendors. The appropriation is expected this Thursday. The

City was awarded $400,000 in state funding for partial warming center operations, which will reduce the amount needed from the City. Several

vendors are involved, including external security, and some remaining funds from last year are available. The City is waiting for the additional funding before finalizing vendor arrangements. In response to Councilor Clingan, Director Carroll confirmed that she does not anticipate any issues with

vendors being ready for the start of operations, as they are familiar with the process.

- Chair McLaughlin expressed surprise that the City was considering moving

the site, particularly given that most of Somerville is residential. He emphasized that the visibility of the unhoused population should not be

viewed as a problem to be solved, while noting that harassment or criminal activity should be taken seriously.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE MARKED WORK

COMPLETED

7. Public

Gilman Square Neighborhood Council submitting comments re: McGrath

Communication Boulevard.

(ID # 26-0493 )

- Chair McLaughlin asked Intergovernmental Affairs Director Amanda

Nagim-Williams to follow up with him about the planned removal of the footbridge and proposed changes to nearby side streets, noting that these

changes could negatively affect the neighborhood. He asked her to review the concerns and report back.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE MARKED WORK

COMPLETED

8. Resolution

By Councilor McLaughlin and Councilor Davis

(ID # 26-0106 ) That the Administration provide monthly updates to the Committee on

- Public Health and Public Safety on progress towards addressing
- homelessness in Somerville.

RESULT: KEPT IN COMMITTEE
